questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a turning point is
questions.learningObjective: state what makes a change a turning point rather than an event
questions.stem: A historian calls a change a turning point. What has to be true of the change for the label to fit?

options.text: The earlier pattern does not resume afterwards, so the change reorganises what follows
The change is the largest of its century, so nothing larger can compare with it
options.misconception: judges importance by size alone

options.text: The change is well documented, so the record leaves no room for argument
options.misconception: confuses a secure record with a structural break

options.text: The change was welcomed by the people it happened to, so it was a real advance
options.misconception: judges a turning point by the applause it received

questions.explanation: A turning point is defined by what does not come back: after it, the older pattern of institutions or economy cannot be restored, so later developments are organised differently. Size, a good record, and popular approval each describe something real about an event without saying anything about whether the earlier order survived it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the old pattern can be put back afterwards.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The cost of choosing a boundary
questions.learningObjective: explain what a chosen period boundary asserts about continuity
questions.stem: Why does picking a date to end one period and begin another commit the historian to a view of the past?

options.text: Because every boundary says which changes broke with the old order and which ran through it
Because every boundary sets a fixed length for the period, so the counting must be exact
options.misconception: treats a scholarly choice as an arithmetic problem

options.text: Because every boundary is drawn by a single event, so only that event can be studied
options.misconception: insists that one event must carry the whole break

options.text: Because every boundary is convenient for teaching, so convenience is the only test
options.misconception: reduces periodisation to the needs of a syllabus

questions.explanation: A boundary is a claim, not a fact: choosing where the old order breaks means declaring which changes were decisive and which were survivable detail, and the same evidence can support different cuts. Exact lengths, a single event, and convenience for teaching are all considerations of a different kind, and none of them is the substance of the claim.
questions.hint: Ask what the boundary asserts about which changes mattered most.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two rival boundaries for the same age
questions.learningObjective: compare what two candidate boundary dates privilege
questions.stem: One course ends the Middle Ages when a great city in the east fell, and another when an ocean crossing returned with a new cargo. What follows from the choice?

options.text: The first privileges a political rupture and the second a commercial one, so the two differ in emphasis
The first is wrong and the second is right, since only a voyage can end an age
options.misconception: rules one out on preference rather than on reasoning

options.text: The two boundaries are the same claim, since a city's fall and a voyage are one event
options.misconception: collapses two distinct events into a single one

options.text: The choice is irrelevant, since a period boundary is a matter of taste with no argument in it
options.misconception: dismisses periodisation as pure preference

questions.explanation: Each boundary is a way of ranking causes: a city's fall to an empire makes the end of the age a matter of politics and war, while a new ocean route makes it a matter of exchange and navigation, and the rest of the course then has to be organised around that emphasis. Neither is simply right, they are not the same claim, and the choice is an argument, not a taste.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of cause each date is being asked to carry.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Continuity against rupture
questions.learningObjective: weigh a continuity account against a rupture account of the same span
questions.stem: One account finds long institutional continuities running from the Middle Ages into modern states; another finds in the same span a series of breaks that left nothing of the earlier order. Which is the better reading?

options.text: Neither alone, because law and religion continue while economy and authority are rebuilt
Continuity alone, because institutions outlast every economic and political change
options.misconception: makes one dimension total and ignores the others

options.text: Rupture alone, because a break in authority erases every continuity that came before
options.misconception: makes one break erase the whole record

options.text: The two are simply different subjects, so no single account of the span is possible at all
options.misconception: calls a failure of judgement a difference of subject

questions.explanation: Continuity and rupture are often claims about different dimensions, and the evidence here separates: law, confession, and office survive changes of regime, while the sources of authority and the economic base are rebuilt more than once. A total continuity, a total rupture, and a refusal to join the dimensions at all each give up what the record plainly shows happening together.
questions.hint: Ask which dimensions of the span change and which survive.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The layers of historical time
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the slow, the medium, and the fast layers of change
questions.stem: A historian distinguishes the slow structures of geography, the medium rhythms of prices and population, and the short span of events and politics. Why separate them?

options.text: Because events sit inside slower processes and cannot be read until the slower ones are dated
Because events are the only layer that a historian is permitted to record at all
options.misconception: privileges the fastest layer as the only recordable one

options.text: Because geography and prices have no effect upon the events that surround them
options.misconception: denies the influence of the slower layers

options.text: Because geography and prices are too remote in time to be studied with any confidence
options.misconception: claims the slowest layers are simply unknowable

questions.explanation: The separation is a claim about causation: an event is intelligible only against the structures and cycles it sits in, and treating the short span as the whole of history is what produces a narrative of pure accident. Only events recordable, no influence from below, and the slow layers unknowable each mistake the arrangement for a limitation.
questions.hint: Ask what an event means once you know the cycle it sits inside.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two accounts of the same age compared
questions.learningObjective: compare two summaries of the late Middle Ages for shared assumptions
questions.stem: One summary describes the later Middle Ages as the slow formation of a European civilisation in which trade, towns, and law grew together. Another describes them as a time of extravagant wealth and anxious ritual, a confident civilisation apprehensive of what was coming.

options.text: Both treat the age as a period with its own character, even though they emphasise different things in it
Both treat the age as a mere prelude with no character before the modern period
options.misconception: denies the shared period claim the summaries make

options.text: They disagree about the dates, since one ends the age before the other begins it
options.misconception: invents a date dispute the summaries never raise

options.text: They disagree about the economy, since one claims trade grew and the other that it stopped
options.misconception: converts a difference of emphasis into direct contradiction

questions.explanation: The two summaries share the basic move of treating this age as a period with its own character rather than a waiting room, and they differ in what they emphasise inside it, one the growth of connections and the other the anxiety behind the display. No shared character, a date dispute, and a contradiction about trade are all disputes the summaries do not have with each other.
questions.hint: Ask what both summaries assume about whether the age has a character.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The year 1000 as a candidate
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a proposed turning point built on demographic evidence
questions.stem: Some historians place a decisive break around the year 1000, when the evidence of population growth and new settlement in western Europe becomes clear. What does that proposal claim?

options.text: That the eleventh century opens a growth phase whose consequences run on into the later ages
That population declined sharply after 1000 and did not recover for three hundred years
options.misconception: inverts the direction of the demographic evidence

options.text: That no farming settlement existed anywhere in Europe before the year 1000
options.misconception: makes a turning point out of the absence of earlier evidence

options.text: That every institution of the later Middle Ages was invented after the year 1000
options.misconception: claims an invention that the record shows beginning earlier

questions.explanation: The proposal reads the turn in the evidence as a real turn in the world: growth in population and settlement opens a phase of clearance, ploughing, and church foundation whose effects run for centuries, which is what a turning point claims to be. A collapse, a blank slate, and a wholesale invention each invert what the same evidence shows.
questions.hint: Ask whether the date marks something beginning or something ending.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Choosing a starting date for modern history
questions.learningObjective: evaluate candidate starting dates for a modern period
questions.stem: Candidates for the beginning of modern history include a city's fall, a return from a voyage with a new cargo, a revolution in one kingdom, and the outbreak of a general war. Which choice is defensible?

options.text: Any of them, provided the date is paired with the criterion that makes it a beginning at all
Only the earliest date, since the first change listed is always the truest beginning
options.misconception: chooses by position in a list rather than by argument

options.text: Only the latest date, since every earlier change was undone by the time it came
options.misconception: treats survival as proof that an earlier change was unreal

options.text: None of them, because any single date leaves out changes that mattered as much as the one chosen
options.misconception: dismisses a working criterion as though only complete lists count

questions.explanation: Each candidate marks a real change, so the defensible move is to state which change the period is said to begin with and to defend that choice against the alternatives, which is what the first option does. Choosing by position in a list, insisting that only the last change counts, and demanding a complete list each reject the whole practice they claim to defend.
questions.hint: Ask what a candidate date is a beginning of, and on whose grounds.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: How the Pirenne thesis works
questions.learningObjective: explain the mechanism of a commercial-rupture thesis
questions.stem: A famous thesis holds that European commerce restarted when a conquering power took an island, because conquest ended the old trading system and isolation then forced a new one. What is the mechanism it proposes?

options.text: Cut the old routes and their users, and the survivors build different ones across the new frontiers
Preserve the old routes, so trade simply continued through the conqueror's own markets
options.misconception: describes continuity where the thesis argues a break

options.text: Close the sea entirely, so trade moved inland to rivers and roads for two centuries
options.misconception: reverses the direction in which trade was rerouted

options.text: End trade altogether for a century, after which the survivors rebuilt it from nothing
options.misconception: makes a complete stoppage the price of the isolation

questions.explanation: The mechanism is a forced rerouting: conquest breaks the established circuits, the old participants lose their positions, and a new generation of towns and merchants grows against the new political map, so the war is what makes the later commerce possible. Preserved routes, a rerouting inland, and a total stoppage each replace the rerouting the thesis actually requires.
questions.hint: Ask what has to happen to a merchant's circuit for a new one to grow.

questions.topic: What the phrase modern period does
questions.learningObjective: state what a period name asserts about its contents
questions.stem: A textbook calls the stretch from about 1500 to the present the modern period. What is the phrase doing for the reader?

options.text: Grouping events under a shared claim that one logic governs them, rather than mere succession
Marking the stretch as the period in which nothing of consequence happened at all
options.misconception: reads a period name as a verdict of emptiness

options.text: Restricting the period to events on the continent, excluding everything else entirely
options.misconception: turns a period name into a geographical exclusion

options.text: Claiming the events inside it are more important than anything before them
options.misconception: converts a grouping into a claim of worth

questions.explanation: A period name is an argument that the events inside it share a governing logic, so the reader is invited to look for connections rather than a list, and that invitation can be tested. Emptiness, geographical exclusion, and a verdict of greater worth are all things the phrase does not claim.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The plague as a candidate turning point
questions.learningObjective: identify the mechanism that makes a demographic shock a turning point
questions.stem: A demographic shock is proposed as a turning point for a region. What makes it a candidate rather than merely a disaster?

options.text: It leaves institutions standing with far fewer people, so survivors inherit and reorganise them
It kills so many that every institution of the period simply disappears with it
options.misconception: assumes total institutional collapse from a large death toll

options.text: It changes the subject matter of historians, who then write about it instead of before it
options.misconception: confuses a change in historical attention with a change in the world

options.text: It ends a period because the deaths are recorded in writing by later chroniclers
options.misconception: makes the survival of a record the cause of a period change

questions.explanation: A shock becomes a turning point when the institutions that carried the work out of it survive on a smaller base, because then property, wages, and obligations are renegotiated by the survivors rather than merely inherited. Institutional disappearance, a change of historical subject, and a change of archive each confuse the aftermath of the shock with the shock itself.
questions.hint: Ask what the survivors inherited and how they changed it.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a demographic shock reorganises an economy
questions.learningObjective: explain the mechanism by which fewer workers change terms
questions.stem: A region loses a large share of its people and, in the following generation, wages rise, rents fall, and rules written for a crowded countryside are broken. Why does that sequence follow?

options.text: Because the land is unchanged while the number of claimants falls, so the bargaining position reverses
Because the survivors abolished the old rules by vote at the very next council
options.misconception: invents a legislative moment that a demographic shock does not provide

options.text: Because the deaths destroyed the land itself, so cultivation was abandoned for a generation
options.misconception: treats a loss of workers as a loss of soil

options.text: Because the old rules were always unpopular, and the deaths only revealed what was already true
options.misconception: makes the new terms a delayed discovery of an old sentiment

questions.explanation: Land does not go anywhere when people die, so the same fields face far fewer claimants, and every old rule that priced labour high or land low is renegotiated by the side with fewer alternatives, which is the whole mechanism in one line. A vote at a council, abandoned cultivation, and an old unpopularity revealed late each insert a cause the arithmetic of the situation does not need.
questions.hint: Ask what stayed the same while the number of people changed.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Counting the gap between two markers
questions.learningObjective: compute the interval between two period markers
questions.stem: A course marks a charter in 1215 and a return from the first ocean crossing in 1492. How many years separate the two markers?

options.text: 277 years, since 1,492 less 1,215 leaves 277
267 years, since the earlier date is subtracted the wrong way and the sign dropped
options.misconception: handles the subtraction as though the order did not matter

options.text: 307 years, since 1,492 is read as though it were 1,522 by transposition
options.misconception: transposes the digits of the later marker

options.text: 387 years, since the difference is taken from the sum of the two dates
options.misconception: adds the two dates and then subtracts nothing

questions.explanation: The interval is 1,492 - 1,215 = 277, which is the whole span between the two markers and is what any statement about the gap has to rest on. Subtracting in the wrong order, transposing the digits of 1,492 into 1,522, and adding the two dates each produce a figure that no route to the difference supports.
questions.hint: Take the later year from the earlier one and do the sum once more.

questions.topic: Justifying a boundary near 1500
questions.learningObjective: compare pairs of changes as evidence for a period boundary
questions.stem: A boundary at about 1500 is defended by pairing a change in print with a change in the routes of trade. Why is a pair stronger evidence than a single event?

Because a pair is easier to fit on one line of a chart than a single event is
options.misconception: prefers what is convenient to display over what is evidence

options.text: Because two events in different spheres prove the earlier order had already ended
options.misconception: infers a finished break from two simultaneous changes

options.text: Because any single event is an accident, while pairs are never accidental at all
options.misconception: dismisses all single events without examining any

Easy to chart, already finished, and never accidental each sound like reasons but settle nothing about the evidence.

questions.topic: Two dates for the Reformation
questions.learningObjective: compare what two candidate Reformation dates mark
questions.stem: One date marks a dispute over indulgences that began a controversy, and a later date marks a settlement that ended a war and fixed the map of churches. Which comparison is fairest?

options.text: The first marks the outbreak of a dispute, the second the settlement that closed it in practice
The first is the true beginning and the later date is a false one invented by opponents
options.misconception: judges the earlier date correct on preference alone

options.text: The first marks the split and the second merely a ceremony, since nothing changed in 1555
options.misconception: reduces a settlement to a ceremony and denies its effects

options.text: The first marks a political revolt and the second a change of currency, so they are unrelated
options.misconception: misdescribes both dates as belonging to other fields

A false date, a mere ceremony, and a change of currency each refuse to let one date do the work the other is doing.
questions.hint: Ask what question each date is meant to answer.

questions.topic: 1789 against 1848
questions.learningObjective: explain how a choice between two dates changes the period's name
questions.stem: A century is called the age of revolution when it begins in 1789, and the age of reform when it begins in 1848. What does the choice decide?

options.text: Whether the century reads as one long revolution or as a reaction ending in a single crisis
Whether the revolutions of 1848 were more violent than those of 1789
options.misconception: reduces a periodisation to a comparison of degrees of violence

options.text: Whether the century's economy grew faster before 1848 than after it
options.misconception: moves the periodisation onto an economic question it cannot settle

options.text: Whether the French monarchy existed in 1789 or only after 1848
options.misconception: answers a question both dates leave settled the same way

Degrees of violence, growth rates, and the existence of a monarchy are real questions, and none of them is the one the choice between the dates answers.
questions.hint: Ask what the century becomes if the climax is early or late.

questions.topic: 1914 and 1945 read as a pair
questions.learningObjective: explain what pairing two wars of one century does to the analysis
questions.stem: A historian treats 1914 and 1939 as the start of one thirty-year crisis rather than two separate wars. What does that framing make visible?

options.text: That the settlements, debts, and institutions left by the first shaped the second's terms
That the two wars had one immediate cause, so the first repeated itself exactly
options.misconception: forces a single cause onto two wars that began differently

options.text: That the years between them were quiet, so nothing links the first to the second
options.misconception: calls an interval of revolution and depression quiet

options.text: That only the second war mattered, since the first settled nothing the second undid
options.misconception: dismisses the first as a cause of the second it explains

questions.topic: Ordering a causal chain of institutions
questions.learningObjective: sequence a chain of steps by which representative institutions grew
questions.stem: Four steps lie between a crown's need for money and a representative body that can refuse it. Put them in the order a causal account requires.

options.text: The claim to be consulted is written into a statute and defended in later decades
options.misconception: puts the negotiated grant before the request for money that the war created

options.text: A representative body acquires the standing to refuse a grant outright
options.misconception: makes the statute the first step, when no claim yet exists to be written into it

options.text: A crown at war asks its subjects for a grant of money it has no right to compel
options.misconception: begins with a refusal that the claim to be consulted has not yet earned

options.misconception: writes the statute before anyone has claimed a right to be consulted

questions.topic: What a bare chronology can establish
questions.learningObjective: state the limit of an undated-commentary chronology
questions.stem: A printed table lists forty events in a single column with their years and no commentary at all. What can a historian safely take from such a table?

options.text: The order and spacing of the events it lists, and nothing about the causes joining them
The causes joining the events, since their order in the column implies the causes
options.misconception: reads a sequence of dates as a chain of causes

options.text: The relative importance of the events, since the earliest entries matter most to a period
options.misconception: infers significance from position in a list

options.text: The attitudes of the people involved, since the dates record how each of them thought
options.misconception: expects a table of dates to carry opinions

That the revolution was caused by something else as well, since one cause is never enough

questions.learningObjective: compute a real wage from two index series
questions.stem: Over a century grain prices rise from an index of 100 to 400, while wages rise from an index of 100 to 160. What happens to what a wage buys?

It falls to four fifths of its earlier level, since the two indices are simply subtracted
